title: Milestone 2 Overview
text:
Milestone 2 Student Study Guides 
 Building the Segmentation Pipeline & First Submission 
 Welcome to Milestone 2 of the Industrial Surface Anomaly Segmentation project! 
 In Milestone 1, you inspected raw annotations, unraveled Run-Length Encoding (RLE) memory layouts, examined the metric penalty on empty masks, and explored the physical constraints of line-scan imaging sensors. In  Milestone 2 , you move from analytical observation to active systems engineering:  designing, training, and validating your first complete deep learning segmentation pipeline, and generating a valid Kaggle submission file . 
 
 1. Prerequisites from Milestone 1 
 Before embarking on Milestone 2, ensure you are comfortable with these core concepts established in Milestone 1: 
 
 Aspect Ratio Awareness : Industrial line-scan images are  \(800 \times 128\)  pixels ( \(6.25:1\)  ratio). You understand why square resizing ( \(256 \times 256\) ) distorts thin longitudinal defects and why native resolutions must be preserved. 
 Fortran-Order RLE Traversal : You understand that RLE strings are 1-indexed and traverse columns from top to bottom ( order='F' ), requiring index clamping at  \(102,400\)  pixels. 
 The Multi-Label Long-Format Schema : You understand that  train.csv  provides four rows per image (one per defect class) and that empty masks represent clean, defect-free material. 
 Metric Sensitivity : You understand the mathematical formulation of the Dice coefficient ( \(F_1\)  score) and the official 70/20/10 weighted competition metric. 
 
 
 2. Curriculum Map: Milestone 2 Topics & Study Guides 
 The six core Milestone 2 competition requirements are organized into eight focused, progressive study guides: 
 
 
 
 Milestone 2 Core Topic 
 Primary Study Guide(s) 
 Theoretical Principles 
 Practical Implementation Focus 
 
 
 
 
 1. Dataset & DataLoader 
 Guide 01: The Dataset Contract Guide 02: Batching & DataLoaders 
 Industrial line-scan geometry, RLE decoding mechanics, tensor contracts  [C,H,W] , multi-process IPC, pinned memory. 
 Build a clean PyTorch  Dataset  and  DataLoader  yielding image  [B, 1, 128, 800]  and mask  [B, 4, 128, 800] . 
 
 
 2. Industrial Augmentations 
 Guide 03: Industrial Augmentations 
 Domain invariances on moving strip, geometric vs photometric duality, mask discreteness, nearest-neighbor interpolation. 
 Implement synchronized horizontal/vertical flips and image-only contrast jitter; diagnose spatial misalignment bugs. 
 
 
 3. Validation Split 
 Guide 04: Multi-Label Stratification 
 The rare-defect "split lottery", hypergeometric sampling variance, combination signatures, data leakage vectors. 
 Create a combination-stratified  \(80/20\)  image-level holdout that guarantees support for rare classes like  defect_b . 
 
 
 4. W&B Experiment Tracking 
 Guide 05: W&B Experiment Tracking 
 The experiment lifecycle, step-axis synchronization, qualitative mask overlays, model artifact lineage, API security. 
 Configure a reproducible W&B logging workflow tracking training loss, validation Dice, and model checkpoints. 
 
 
 5. Baseline U-Net & Training 
 Guide 06: Baseline U-Net & Training 
 Encoder-decoder contracting/expanding paths, skip connections, BCE + Soft Dice compound loss, optimization lifecycle. 
 Implement and train a baseline U-Net for 5–10 epochs; monitor loss convergence and save the best checkpoint. 
 
 
 6. Prediction, RLE & Submission 
 Guide 07: Logits to Binary Masks Guide 08: RLE & First Submission 
 Probability thresholding  \(\tau\) , 8-connected components, minimum area filtering  \(A_{\min}\) , Fortran RLE, single-space sentinel. 
 Calibrate post-processing thresholds, encode binary masks to RLE strings, and generate a 12,001-row submission CSV. 
 
 
 
 
 3. Guide Overviews & Learning Sequence 
 Follow this recommended reading and implementation sequence: 
 
 
 Guide 01: The Dataset Contract: From Annotation Rows to Aligned Strip Tensors :
  Traces fictional image  STRIP_0042  from raw JPEG and CSV rows through grayscale loading, Fortran RLE decoding, boundary clamping, and 4-channel mask stacking. Teaches the empirical mask overlap audit. 
 
 
 Guide 02: Batching, DataLoaders, and Image-Level Isolation :
  Explains how PyTorch's  DataLoader  collates tensors into 4D minibatches  [B, C, H, W] , details worker seeding with  worker_init_fn , and proves why splitting must occur strictly at the  image ID level  to prevent catastrophic row-level leakage. 
 
 
 Guide 03: Industrial Augmentations: Geometric Alignment and Photometric Invariance :
  Separates geometric transforms (applied to image and mask identically) from photometric transforms (applied to image only). Discusses the physical plausibility of horizontal vs. vertical flips on steel strips and demonstrates why masks require nearest-neighbor interpolation. 
 
 
 Guide 04: Validation Strategy: Multi-Label Stratification for Rare Defect Detection :
  Demonstrates how naive random splits cause severe variance for rare defects (like  defect_b ), introduces multi-label combination stratification, and provides a strict data leakage prevention checklist. 
 
 
 Guide 05: Experiment Tracking with Weights & Biases :
  Walks through the complete W&B experiment lifecycle: configuration logging, step axis synchronization, interactive qualitative mask overlays, model artifact versioning, and secure API key management. 
 
 
 Guide 06: Baseline Segmentation with U-Net: Architecture, Heads, and Optimization :
  Dissects U-Net's contracting path, bottleneck, expanding path, and skip connections. Traces feature map shapes for a  \(128 \times 800\)  strip, contrasts 4-Sigmoid vs. 5-Softmax heads, details the BCE + Soft Dice compound loss, and guides a modest 5-epoch sanity run. 
 
 
 Guide 07: Post-Processing & The Decision Pipeline: Logits to Binary Masks :
  Explains how to bridge continuous model logits to binary masks via decision thresholds  \(\tau\) , analyzes connected components with OpenCV, and applies minimum area filtering ( \(A_{\min}\) ) to suppress sensor noise speckles. 
 
 
 Guide 08: Run-Length Encoding and First Kaggle Submission :
  Details the 1-indexed column-major Fortran RLE encoding algorithm, explains the mandatory single-space sentinel ( " " ) for empty masks, and provides a 7-point pre-submission validation checklist to guarantee Kaggle acceptance. 
 
 
 
 4. Standalone Code Examples & Synthetic Walkthrough 
 To support hands-on learning without disclosing competition training results, this curriculum includes complete, self-contained educational resources built entirely on  synthetic data : 
 1. Interactive Walkthrough Notebook 
 
 Jupyter Notebook :  notebooks/synthetic_pipeline_walkthrough.ipynb 
 Paired Python Script :  notebooks/synthetic_pipeline_walkthrough.py 
 Notebook Setup Guide :  notebooks/README.md 
 
 This walkthrough runs on CPU in under 5 seconds and demonstrates every stage of the pipeline from synthetic strip generation to U-Net optimization and RLE encoding. 
 2. Standalone Diagnostic Scripts 
 
 
 Dataset & Batching Diagnostic :  examples/toy_dataset_loader.py 
  Validates  __getitem__  tensor shapes, normalization, and DataLoader collation. 
 
 
 RLE Roundtrip Diagnostic :  examples/toy_rle_roundtrip.py 
  Verifies column-major RLE encoding, empty-mask single-space handling, and boundary clamping. 
 
 
 U-Net Optimization Lifecycle :  examples/toy_unet_step.py 
  Executes a forward pass, BCE loss calculation, backward pass, and optimizer step on a lightweight 2-level U-Net on CPU. 
 
 
 
 5. Teaching Philosophy and Boundaries 
 These study guides are designed as a  guiding hand, not a shortcut : 
 
 They explain the underlying mathematics, tensor dimensions, software interfaces, failure modes, and debugging techniques. 
 They do  not  provide a copy-paste competition training script, pre-computed hyperparameter values, or trained model checkpoints. 
 They do  not  reveal confidential exploratory data analysis findings or performance benchmarks from the private training set. 
 You must write, audit, and debug your own segmentation pipeline against  data/public/ .

title: Guide 01 · The Dataset Contract
text:
The Dataset Contract: From Annotation Rows to Aligned Strip Tensors 
 In Milestone 1, you explored the dataset's geometry, the Fortran-order conventions of Run-Length Encoding (RLE), and the mathematical behavior of segmentation metrics on empty masks. In Milestone 2, you move from exploration to execution: building a robust, high-performance deep learning pipeline. 
 The foundation of every deep learning pipeline is the PyTorch  Dataset . If your data loading pipeline silently swaps image dimensions, misaligns defect masks with visual textures, or confuses defect channels, no sophisticated network architecture can rescue your model. This guide establishes the  dataset contract  required for industrial strip anomaly segmentation. 
 
 1. Motivation: The Industrial Strip Imaging Context 
 In industrial manufacturing facilities (such as steel cold-rolling mills), surface quality is continuously monitored by high-speed line-scan cameras positioned above conveyor lines. These cameras capture optical sensor frames with extreme aspect ratios:  800 pixels wide by 128 pixels high  (an aspect ratio of  \(6.25:1\) ). 
 Conveyor Motion (Strip Length / Rolling Axis) ──────────────────────────► Width = 800 px
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                    [Line-Scan Sensor]                                 │ Height = 128 px
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 
 When building a computer vision model for this domain, standard computer vision assumptions break down: 
 
 Sensors are Anisotropic : Objects do not appear in square  \(256 \times 256\)  or  \(512 \times 512\)  scenes. Resizing an  \(800 \times 128\)  strip to a square alters physical scale ratios by over  \(600\%\) , crushing thin longitudinal scratches into aliasing artifacts. 
 Annotations are Multi-Label & Long-Format : Each visual strip can contain multiple defects or none at all. In  train.csv , annotations are provided as multiple rows per image. 
 Channels are Monochromatic : Steel strips are optically recorded as single-channel grayscale intensity values, not RGB color photos. 
 
 The PyTorch  Dataset  must bridge this raw disk storage and the tensor format expected by 2D convolutional neural networks: converting disk images and RLE strings into perfectly aligned tensors of shape  \([C, H, W]\) . 
 
 2. Tracing One Sample: The Data Contract 
 Let us trace a single fictional sample,  image_id = "STRIP_0042" , from disk to PyTorch tensor. 
 Step 1: Disk Storage & Schema 
 On disk, raw images reside as JPEG files at  data/public/train/{image_id}.jpg . Their annotations reside in  data/public/train.csv , where every image possesses four rows—one for each defect category:

 Notice that empty defects appear as  NaN  or empty strings, while active defects provide a space-delimited RLE string. 
 Step 2: Grayscale Image Loading 
 Because line-scan inspection images are monochromatic, load the image using OpenCV in grayscale mode:
 image = cv2.imread(image_path, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)  # Returns ndarray of shape (128, 800), uint8 
Loading in default BGR mode ( cv2.imread(image_path) ) creates three identical redundant color channels, tripling memory bandwidth and VRAM usage without providing additional physical information. 
 Step 3: Fortran-Order RLE Decoding 
 The RLE strings follow the standard Kaggle/Severstal specification: 
 
 1-indexed : Pixel counting begins at index 1 (not 0). 
 Column-Major (Fortran order,  order='F' ) : Pixels are traversed top-to-bottom down column 0, then top-to-bottom down column 1, and so forth. 
 Pairs : Alternating  start length  values. 
 
 Mathematically, for a canvas of height  \(H=128\)  and width  \(W=800\) , a 1-indexed linear index  \(k \in \{1, \dots, H \times W\}\)  maps to 0-indexed row coordinate  \(r\)  and column coordinate  \(c\)  via: 
 \[c = \left\lfloor \frac{k - 1}{H} \right\rfloor, \quad r = (k - 1) \pmod{H}\] 
 Linear Pixel 1  ──► (r=0, c=0)
Linear Pixel 2  ──► (r=1, c=0)
...
Linear Pixel 128 ─► (r=127, c=0)
Linear Pixel 129 ─► (r=0, c=1) 
 Step 4: The Boundary Clamping Safety Rule 
 When decoding real-world segmentation masks, boundary rounding can produce a run whose endpoint exceeds total pixels: 
 \[k_{\text{end}} = k_{\text{start}} + L\] 
 On a canvas of  \(128 \times 800 = 102,400\)  pixels, an index  \(k_{\text{end}} > 102,400\)  causes an out-of-bounds  IndexError  when reshaped. Your decoder must clamp: 
 \[k_{\text{clamped\_end}} = \min(k_{\text{start}} + L - 1, H \times W)\] 
 Step 5: Multi-Channel Target Stacking 
 Because each image can exhibit any combination of the four defect classes, we construct a 4-channel binary target tensor: 
 \[\mathbf{Y} \in \{0.0, 1.0\}^{4 \times 128 \times 800}\] 
 Channels must follow a strict, deterministic ordering across your entire codebase: 
 
 Channel 0:  defect_a 
 Channel 1:  defect_b 
 Channel 2:  defect_c 
 Channel 3:  defect_d 
 
 
 Figure 1.1: Tracing image  STRIP_0042  from CSV rows and JPEG disk file through RLE decoding into aligned PyTorch tensors.

 4. Ground Truth Exclusivity: The Multi-Label Audit 
 Before deciding whether your network should use 4 independent Sigmoid outputs or a 5-class mutually-exclusive Softmax output (background + 4 defects), you must answer an empirical question: 
 \[\text{Do ground-truth defect masks ever overlap at the exact same pixel?}\] 
 For any pair of active masks  \(M_i, M_j \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W}\)  on image  \(k\) : 
 \[\text{Overlap}_{i, j} = \sum_{r=0}^{H-1} \sum_{c=0}^{W-1} \left( M_i(r, c) \cdot M_j(r, c) \right)\] 
 
 If  \(\text{Overlap}_{i, j} = 0\)  for all pairs across all images, the defect masks are strictly  pixel-disjoint . 
 If  \(\text{Overlap}_{i, j} > 0\)  for some images, the defect masks are  spatially overlapping . 
 
 Do not assume either outcome based on intuition or past Kaggle competitions. Write an audit script that iterates through every multi-defect image in  train.csv  and computes pairwise mask intersections. Your empirical finding will dictate whether a 5-channel Softmax head is mathematically permissible. 
 
 5. Dataset Architecture & Interface 
 In PyTorch, a clean  Dataset  encapsulates storage access and exposes two required methods:  __len__  and  __getitem__ . 
 The  __getitem__  Interface Contract 
 When  dataset[idx]  is evaluated, it should return a structured dictionary:
 sample = {
    "image_id": str,          # Fictional ID for tracking and validation
    "image": torch.Tensor,    # Shape: [1, 128, 800], dtype: torch.float32
    "mask": torch.Tensor,     # Shape: [4, 128, 800], dtype: torch.float32
} 
 PyTorch Tensor Convention: [Channels, Height, Width]
- Image: [1, 128, 800] ──► 1 grayscale channel, 128 rows, 800 columns
- Mask:  [4, 128, 800] ──► 4 defect channels, 128 rows, 800 columns 
 Image Normalization Strategy 
 Raw sensor pixels range from 0 to 255. Feeding unnormalized integers into neural networks destabilizes weight initialization and gradient descent. Two standard normalization strategies exist: 
 
 
 Min-Max Scaling to  \([0, 1]\) : 
 \[x_{\text{norm}} = \frac{x}{255.0}\] 
 
 
 Per-Dataset Standardization (Z-score) : 
 \[x_{\text{norm}} = \frac{x / 255.0 - \mu}{\sigma}\] 
 where  \(\mu\)  and  \(\sigma\)  are the empirical mean and standard deviation of your training partition. 
 
 
 Whichever strategy you select,  compute  \(\mu\)  and  \(\sigma\)  only on the training partition , never across the full dataset, to prevent subtle data leakage. 
 
 6. Common Mistakes and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Pitfall 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Practical Diagnostic 
 
 
 
 
 Transposed Dimensions 
 Passing shape as  (800, 128)  instead of  (128, 800) . 
 Reshape error or vertically stretched, sheared masks. 
 Assert  sample["image"].shape == (1, 128, 800)  in  __getitem__ . 
 
 
 C-Order RLE Decode 
 Using  order='C'  instead of  order='F'  in NumPy reshape. 
 Defect mask appears diagonally sheared and misaligned with the visual flaw. 
 Overlay decoded mask onto the image and verify visual alignment on defect features. 
 
 
 Silent Channel Permutation 
 Iterating over an unsorted dictionary of defect rows. 
 Channel 0 is sometimes  defect_a , sometimes  defect_c . Loss fails to converge. 
 Enforce a fixed class list:  CLASSES = ["defect_a", "defect_b", "defect_c", "defect_d"] . 
 
 
 Mask Blurring 
 Loading masks with bilinear interpolation during preprocessing. 
 Binary masks contain fractional values ( \(0.34, 0.78\) ). 
 Check  torch.unique(sample["mask"])  contains only  \(\{0.0, 1.0\}\) . 
 
 
 Off-by-One RLE Shift 
 Forgetting that Kaggle RLE is 1-indexed ( start - 1 ). 
 Mask is shifted by 1 pixel along the column traversal. 
 Decode a toy RLE string  "1 2"  and check that pixels at index 0 and 1 are active. 
 
 
 
 
 7. Design Decisions You Must Make 
 Before proceeding to batching and model training, collect empirical evidence to guide these decisions: 
 
 Target Semantics : Will you format ground truth targets as four independent binary channels  [4, 128, 800]  (for Sigmoid/BCE), or as a single multi-class integer map  [128, 800]  with class indices  \(\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\)  (for Softmax/Cross-Entropy)? 
 Evidence required : Your empirical pairwise mask overlap audit. 
 
 
 
 Caching Strategy : The training set contains 11,393 images ( \(128 \times 800\)  uint8). Uncompressed, all images occupy: 
 \[11,393 \times 128 \times 800 \text{ bytes} \approx 1.17 \text{ GB}\] 
 Can your system RAM comfortably hold ~1.2 GB of raw image arrays in memory to eliminate disk I/O bottlenecks during training epochs? 
 
 
 Channel Ordering : Document your channel index mapping in a centralized configuration file to guarantee model heads, metric calculators, and submission encoders agree. 
 
 
 
 8. Try It: Verify Sample Alignment on Toy Data 
 Run this self-contained diagnostic snippet in your terminal or scratch script to inspect mask decoding and tensor alignment on a toy  \(4 \times 6\)  canvas: 
 import numpy as np
import torch

def decode_toy_rle(rle_str, shape=(4, 6)):
    tokens = [int(x) for x in rle_str.split()]
    starts = np.array(tokens[0::2]) - 1  # Convert 1-indexed to 0-indexed
    lengths = np.array(tokens[1::2])
    flat = np.zeros(shape[0] * shape[1], dtype=np.uint8)
    for s, l in zip(starts, lengths):
        flat[s : s + l] = 1
    return flat.reshape(shape, order="F")

# Toy defect in column 2 (rows 1 and 2): linear indices 10 and 11
toy_rle = "10 2"
mask_2d = decode_toy_rle(toy_rle, shape=(4, 6))

print("Decoded 4x6 Mask (order='F'):")
print(mask_2d)
assert mask_2d[1, 2] == 1 and mask_2d[2, 2] == 1, "Pixel alignment failed!"
assert mask_2d.sum() == 2, "Decoded pixel count mismatch!"
print("✓ Toy alignment verified successfully!")

👉  docs/milestone_2_student_guide/examples/toy_dataset_loader.py

title: Guide 02 · Batching & DataLoaders
text:
Batching, DataLoaders, and Image-Level Isolation 
 Once your PyTorch  Dataset  can reliably decode individual images and defect masks into  [C, H, W]  tensors, the next engineering challenge is feeding them efficiently into your neural network. Modern deep learning accelerators (GPUs and TPUs) rely on  batched tensor operations  to achieve massive parallel throughput. 
 In this guide, you will learn how the PyTorch  DataLoader  collates individual samples into 4D batch tensors, how multi-process worker mechanics function, and why  image-level isolation  is the single most critical guardrail against subtle validation data leakage. 
 
 1. Motivation: The Mechanics of Batching 
 Training a neural network with individual images ( \(B=1\) ) is computationally inefficient. GPUs contain thousands of compute cores designed for SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operations. Minibatch gradient descent averages gradients across  \(B\)  independent samples, reducing gradient variance and allowing large matrix multiplications: 
 \[\mathbf{X}_{\text{batch}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times H \times W}, \quad \mathbf{Y}_{\text{batch}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times K \times H \times W}\] 
 For our industrial strip dataset, this translates to: 
 
 Input Image Batch:  \([B, 1, 128, 800]\)  in  torch.float32 
 Target Mask Batch:  \([B, 4, 128, 800]\)  in  torch.float32 
 
 Managing this batch assembly requires careful orchestration of CPU multiprocessing, system memory pinning, and GPU data transfers. 
 
 2. Image-Level Isolation: The Long-Format Split Hazard 
 In standard computer vision datasets, each row in an annotation CSV typically corresponds to a distinct image. In our industrial surface anomaly dataset,  each image spans four consecutive rows  in  train.csv  (one per defect class). 
 train.csv Row Layout:
Row 0: STRIP_0001, defect_a, NaN
Row 1: STRIP_0001, defect_b, NaN
Row 2: STRIP_0001, defect_c, "100 20 ..."  <-- Same physical image!
Row 3: STRIP_0001, defect_d, NaN
Row 4: STRIP_0002, defect_a, NaN
... 
 The Catastrophic Failure: Row-Level Random Splitting 
 If you apply a naive splitting function (such as  sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split ) directly to the rows of  train.csv , rows belonging to  STRIP_0001  will be randomly distributed across both partitions: 
 
 Train Split: receives Row 0 ( defect_a ), Row 1 ( defect_b ), Row 3 ( defect_d ) 
 Validation Split: receives Row 2 ( defect_c ) 
 
 What happens during training? 
 
 The training loop loads  STRIP_0001.jpg  from disk and updates weights based on rows 0, 1, and 3. 
 The validation loop loads  STRIP_0001.jpg  and evaluates row 2. 
 Because the network has already observed the exact physical surface texture, rolling grain, and lighting of  STRIP_0001.jpg  during training, your validation metrics will appear artificially high. 
 Golden Rule of Dataset Splitting:  The train/validation split must take place at the  Image ID level , strictly  before  instantiating any  Dataset  or  DataLoader  objects. 
 
 
 
 \[\text{Train}_{\text{IDs}} \cap \text{Val}_{\text{IDs}} = \emptyset\] 
 # The Disjoint Isolation Assertion
train_ids = set(train_dataset.image_ids)
val_ids = set(val_dataset.image_ids)
assert len(train_ids.intersection(val_ids)) == 0, "FATAL DATA LEAK: Overlapping image IDs detected!" 
 
 3. The DataLoader Architecture 
 The PyTorch  DataLoader  manages asynchronous multi-process loading and tensor collation. 
 
 Figure 2.1: Multi-process DataLoader execution flow: worker processes load and transform samples in parallel, passing them to the main process for collation, memory pinning, and non-blocking GPU transfer. 
 Key DataLoader Parameters: 
 1.  batch_size 
 Determines the number of samples grouped into one forward/backward pass. 
 
 Larger batch sizes ( \(B=16, 32\) ) stabilize batch normalization statistics and increase GPU utilization. 
 Smaller batch sizes ( \(B=4, 8\) ) consume less VRAM and introduce stochastic regularization, but increase gradient variance. 
 
 2.  shuffle 
 
 Training : Set  shuffle=True . Randomizing the sequence of samples prevents cyclical optimization paths and breaks correlations between adjacent batches. 
 Validation : Set  shuffle=False . Validation evaluates fixed model performance on a static dataset; shuffling adds unnecessary CPU overhead. 
 
 3.  num_workers 
 Controls the number of background worker subprocesses spawned to load images and decode RLE masks. 
 
 num_workers=0 : Data loading occurs synchronously in the main Python process. The GPU sits completely idle while the CPU reads images from disk and runs augmentations. 
 num_workers=2  or  4 : Background processes pre-load upcoming batches while the GPU computes the current forward/backward pass. 
 
 4.  pin_memory=True 
 Allocates batch tensors in host  page-locked (pinned) system memory . 
 
 Pinned memory bypasses OS virtual memory paging, enabling hardware Direct Memory Access (DMA) controllers to stream data directly into GPU VRAM. 
 Paired with  batch["image"].to(device, non_blocking=True) , data transfers execute concurrently with GPU kernel execution. 
 
 5.  worker_init_fn : Reproducibility Across Subprocesses 
 When using multi-worker data loading, Python's  random  and NumPy's  np.random  generators in worker processes inherit identical seeds from the parent process by default. Without an explicit  worker_init_fn , every worker process will apply the exact same sequence of random augmentations! 
 def seed_worker(worker_id):
    worker_seed = torch.initial_seed() % 2**32
    np.random.seed(worker_seed)
    random.seed(worker_seed) 
 
 4. Batch Memory Footprint Calculations 
 Before selecting a batch size, calculate your tensor memory requirements. For a batch of size  \(B\)  with single-channel images and 4-channel masks: 
 \[\text{Image Memory} = B \times 1 \times 128 \times 800 \times 4 \text{ bytes} = B \times 409,600 \text{ bytes} \approx B \times 0.40 \text{ MB}\] 
 \[\text{Mask Memory} = B \times 4 \times 128 \times 800 \times 4 \text{ bytes} = B \times 1,638,400 \text{ bytes} \approx B \times 1.60 \text{ MB}\]

 Notice that the raw batch tensors are lightweight. The primary VRAM consumer during training is  intermediate activation feature maps  retained for backpropagation, not the input batch itself. 
 
 5. Custom Collation: Why Default Collate Works 
 By default, PyTorch uses  torch.utils.data.dataloader.default_collate . If your  Dataset.__getitem__  returns a dictionary:
 {
    "image_id": "STRIP_0042",
    "image": torch.Tensor(1, 128, 800),
    "mask": torch.Tensor(4, 128, 800)
} 
The  default_collate  function inspects the types: 
 
 torch.Tensor  objects are stacked along a new 0th dimension:  \([B, 1, 128, 800]\)  and  \([B, 4, 128, 800]\) . 
 Strings ( image_id ) are assembled into a Python list of strings:  ["STRIP_0042", "STRIP_0043", ...] . 
 
 You only need a custom  collate_fn  if you introduce variable-length metadata or bounding boxes. For fixed-size industrial strip tensors,  default_collate  is optimal. 
 
 6. Common Mistakes and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Failure Mode 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Practical Diagnostic 
 
 
 
 
 Row-Level Leakage 
 Splitting  train.csv  rows directly without grouping by  image_id . 
 Validation score starts at  \(>0.85\)  on epoch 1, but test score is near 0. 
 Assert  len(set(train_ids) & set(val_ids)) == 0 . 
 
 
 Worker Process Deadlock 
 OpenCV multi-threading conflicting with PyTorch multiprocessing fork. 
 DataLoader freezes indefinitely on batch 1 with 100% CPU usage. 
 Call  cv2.setNumThreads(0)  at the beginning of your script. 
 
 
 Identical Augmentation Streams 
 Omitting  worker_init_fn  with multi-worker loading. 
 Workers apply identical augmentations to different images. 
 Inspect random numbers generated inside workers across epochs. 
 
 
 VRAM Out-of-Memory (OOM) 
 Batch size too large for GPU VRAM during backward pass. 
 RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory  during  loss.backward() . 
 Halve your  batch_size  or use gradient accumulation. 
 
 
 Unshuffled Training Batches 
 Setting  shuffle=False  on the training  DataLoader . 
 Training loss oscillates erratically or plateaus early. 
 Verify  shuffle=True  on training loader,  shuffle=False  on validation loader. 
 
 
 
 
 7. Decisions You Must Make 
 
 Worker Count Tuning : Benchmark data loading speed on your training machine: 
 Run 100 batches with  num_workers=0, 2, 4 . 
 Measure batches loaded per second:  \(\text{throughput} = \frac{N_{\text{batches}}}{\text{elapsed\_time}}\) . 
 Select the lowest worker count that saturates your GPU without consuming excessive system RAM. 
 
 
 Batch Size vs. Gradient Accumulation : If your target GPU has limited VRAM (e.g., 8 GB or 16 GB), you may be constrained to  \(B=4\)  or  \(B=8\) . If you require the gradient stability of  \(B=16\) , implement  gradient accumulation :
    # Simulate effective batch size = micro_batch * accumulation_steps
loss = loss / accumulation_steps
loss.backward()
if (step + 1) % accumulation_steps == 0:
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad() 
 
 
 8. Try It: Verify Batch Collation and Isolation on Toy Data 
 Run this self-contained diagnostic snippet to verify that your DataLoader collates tensors properly and that your train/val partitions are strictly isolated: 
 import pandas as pd
import torch
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

class ToyDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, ids):
        self.ids = ids
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.ids)
    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        return {
            "image_id": self.ids[idx],
            "image": torch.full((1, 128, 800), idx, dtype=torch.float32),
            "mask": torch.zeros((4, 128, 800), dtype=torch.float32),
        }

# Fictional image IDs
all_ids = [f"STRIP_{i:04d}" for i in range(10)]

# Image-level 80/20 split
train_ids = all_ids[:8]
val_ids = all_ids[8:]

# 1. Isolation check
assert len(set(train_ids).intersection(set(val_ids))) == 0, "Leakage detected!"
print(f"Split verified: {len(train_ids)} train images, {len(val_ids)} val images. Disjoint: TRUE.")

# 2. Batch collation check
train_loader = DataLoader(ToyDataset(train_ids), batch_size=4, shuffle=True)
batch = next(iter(train_loader))

print(f"Batch images shape: {tuple(batch['image'].shape)} [B, C, H, W]")
print(f"Batch masks shape:  {tuple(batch['mask'].shape)} [B, C, H, W]")
print(f"Batch IDs:          {batch['image_id']}")
assert batch["image"].shape == (4, 1, 128, 800), "Image batch shape error!"
assert batch["mask"].shape == (4, 4, 128, 800), "Mask batch shape error!"
print("✓ DataLoader batch collation verified successfully!")

title: Guide 03 · Industrial Augmentations
text:
Industrial Augmentations: Geometric Alignment and Photometric Invariance 
 Data augmentation is one of the most effective techniques for preventing neural networks from overfitting to training data. By synthetically expanding the variety of training samples, augmentations teach your model which variations represent meaningless noise and which represent genuine visual patterns. 
 However, in  semantic segmentation of industrial materials , data augmentation introduces critical failure modes that do not exist in standard image classification. If an augmentation transforms an image without transforming its corresponding mask identically, or if an interpolation algorithm blurs discrete defect boundaries, your model will be trained on corrupted labels. 
 This guide explores the physics of industrial line-scan imagery, separates geometric from photometric transformations, and demonstrates how to guarantee strict spatial alignment between images and masks. 
 
 1. Motivation: Domain Invariances in Line-Scan Imaging 
 When training a model to detect defects on cold-rolled steel strips, consider the physical mechanics of the production line: 
 Direction of Rolling (Conveyor Translation) ──────────────────────────►
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                       │ Top Strip Edge
│   ≈≈≈≈≈ Longitudinal Roll Scratch ≈≈≈≈≈                              │
│                                           ● Staining Cluster         │
│                                                                       │ Bottom Strip Edge
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 
 
 Longitudinal Translation Invariance : A roll scratch occurring at column  \(x=150\)  is physically identical in nature to a scratch occurring at column  \(x=650\) . The defect's nature does not depend on its position along the conveyor. 
 Transverse Edge Invariance : The top edge and bottom edge of the strip experience similar thermal and mechanical stresses. A defect appearing near the top boundary could just as plausibly appear near the bottom boundary. 
 Lighting & Surface Finish Variability : Minor fluctuations in factory ambient lighting, coil surface reflectivity, or sensor exposure alter pixel brightness and contrast without altering defect morphology. 
 
 An effective augmentation pipeline injects these realistic physical variations while strictly respecting sensor constraints. 
 
 2. Categorizing Augmentations: Geometric vs. Photometric 
 Augmentations must be strictly divided into two distinct mathematical categories: 
                        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                       │          Augmentation Pipeline          │
                       └────────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                            │
                     ┌──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┐
                     ▼                                             ▼
       ┌───────────────────────────┐                 ┌───────────────────────────┐
       │   Geometric Transforms    │                 │   Photometric Transforms  │
       ├───────────────────────────┤                 ├───────────────────────────┤
       │ • Horizontal Flip (p=0.5) │                 │ • Contrast Adjust (γ, α)  │
       │ • Vertical Flip (p=0.5)   │                 │ • Brightness Jitter       │
       │ • Shifts / Small Crops    │                 │ • Gaussian Sensor Noise   │
       ├───────────────────────────┤                 ├───────────────────────────┤
       │ APPLIED TO:               │                 │ APPLIED TO:               │
       │ Image AND Mask Identically│                 │ Image ONLY!               │
       └───────────────────────────┘                 └───────────────────────────┘ 
 1. Geometric Transforms (Dual Transformation) 
 Geometric transforms alter spatial pixel coordinates  \((x, y) \mapsto (x', y')\) . 
 
 Examples: Horizontal flip, vertical flip, horizontal translation. 
 
 Rule : Whenever coordinates are shifted, reflected, or cropped, the  exact same coordinate mapping must be applied to every channel of the mask : 
 \[\mathbf{X}_{\text{aug}} = T_{\text{geom}}(\mathbf{X}), \quad \mathbf{Y}_{\text{aug}} = T_{\text{geom}}(\mathbf{Y})\] 
 
 
 2. Photometric Transforms (Image-Only Transformation) 
 Photometric transforms alter pixel intensity values  \(I(x, y) \mapsto f(I(x, y))\)  while leaving spatial coordinates unchanged. 
 
 Examples: Random brightness, contrast adjustment, gamma correction, Gaussian noise. 
 Rule : Intensity changes must be applied  exclusively to the image . Applying a brightness adjustment or contrast curve to a binary mask corrupts ground-truth  \(\{0.0, 1.0\}\)  indicator values into invalid, meaningless floats! 
 
 
 3. Physical Plausibility of Transforms on Industrial Strips 
 Not every transformation that works on ImageNet natural images is physically sound for industrial line-scan strips. 
 
 
 
 Transformation 
 Physical Validity on  \(128 \times 800\)  Strips 
 Rationale 
 
 
 
 
 Horizontal Flip ( p=0.5 ) 
 Highly Plausible 
 Steel coils can be inspected moving forward or backward; reflection along the rolling axis preserves strip geometry and scratch orientation. 
 
 
 Vertical Flip ( p=0.5 ) 
 Plausible 
 Inverts the top and bottom edges of the strip. Defect formation physics are largely symmetric across the sheet width. 
 
 
 \(90^\circ\)  or  \(270^\circ\)  Rotation 
 INVALID 
 Rotating by  \(90^\circ\)  produces an  \(800 \times 128\)  image. Industrial line-scan cameras have fixed mounting geometries; strips never travel sideways. 
 
 
 Square Resize ( \(256 \times 256\) ) 
 HARMFUL 
 Crushes the natural  \(6.25:1\)  aspect ratio, compressing width by  \(3.125\times\)  while expanding height by  \(2.0\times\) . Fine longitudinal cracks are obliterated by aliasing. 
 
 
 Arbitrary Continuous Rotation 
 Questionable 
 Rotating by arbitrary angles (e.g.,  \(15^\circ\) ) introduces large black boundary triangles on wide strips and requires interpolation. 
 
 
 
 
 4. Mask Discreteness and the Interpolation Hazard 
 When an augmentation library scales, rotates, or shifts an image, it must compute pixel values at fractional coordinate locations  \((x + \delta x, y + \delta y)\)  using  interpolation . 
 Input Image (Continuous Float) ──────► Bilinear / Bicubic Interpolation (Smooth)
Input Mask  (Discrete Binary)  ──────► NEAREST NEIGHBOR ONLY! (Preserves {0, 1}) 
 The Bilinear Mask Bug 
 Bilinear interpolation calculates a weighted average of four neighboring pixels: 
 \[I(x, y) = (1 - \Delta x)(1 - \Delta y) I_{00} + \Delta x(1 - \Delta y) I_{10} + (1 - \Delta x)\Delta y I_{01} + \Delta x \Delta y I_{11}\] 
 If applied to a binary mask where neighboring pixels are 0 and 1, bilinear interpolation produces fractional edge values: 
 \[M(x, y) \in \{0.0, 0.23, 0.45, 0.78, 1.0\}\] 
 A binary ground truth mask must represent a deterministic binary statement:  defect is present (1)  or  defect is absent (0) . Fractional values corrupt cross-entropy and Dice loss calculations. 
 
 Crucial Rule:  Always specify  interpolation=cv2.INTER_NEAREST  (or  cv2.INTER_NEAREST_EXACT ) for segmentation masks. For input images, use  cv2.INTER_LINEAR  or  cv2.INTER_CUBIC . 
 
 
 5. Visual Bug Diagnosis: Aligned vs. Broken Augmentations 
 Observe the visual contrast between a correctly synchronized augmentation and two standard augmentation bugs: 
 
 Figure 3.1: Visual alignment diagnosis. (A) Original image with defect mask. (B) Correct joint horizontal flip: image and mask flipped together. (C) Broken unsynchronized flip: image flipped but mask untouched, highlighting pristine steel. (D) Broken interpolation: bilinear filtering blurs mask boundaries. 
 Why the Unsynchronized Bug (Figure 3.1 C) Destroys Models: 
 When the image is flipped horizontally but the mask is left unflipped: 
 
 The network sees visual defect features on the right side of the image, but the target mask tells the network that the label there is  0 (pristine background) . 
 The target mask tells the network that there is a  defect on the left side , where the visual pixels show completely clean steel. 
 The loss function severely penalizes the network when it correctly detects the defect, while forcing it to hallucinate anomalies on clean steel. Training diverges. 
 
 
 6. Implementation Pattern: Dual Augmentation 
 When building your augmentation pipeline (whether using Albumentations or custom NumPy functions), ensure that random decisions are shared between image and mask: 
 import numpy as np
import cv2

def apply_industrial_augmentations(
    image: np.ndarray,      # Shape: (128, 800), uint8
    masks: np.ndarray,      # Shape: (4, 128, 800), float32
    hflip_prob: float = 0.5,
    vflip_prob: float = 0.5,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Apply synchronized geometric flips and image-only photometric augmentations."""

    # 1. Synchronized Horizontal Flip
    if np.random.rand() < hflip_prob:
        image = np.fliplr(image)
        masks = np.flip(masks, axis=2)  # Flip along width axis (axis 2 of [C, H, W])

    # 2. Synchronized Vertical Flip
    if np.random.rand() < vflip_prob:
        image = np.flipud(image)
        masks = np.flip(masks, axis=1)  # Flip along height axis (axis 1 of [C, H, W])

    # 3. Photometric Augmentations (Applied to IMAGE ONLY)
    # Example: Random Contrast Adjustment (gamma scaling)
    if np.random.rand() < 0.3:
        gamma = np.random.uniform(0.8, 1.2)
        # Intensity mapping on image only
        inv_gamma = 1.0 / gamma
        table = np.array([((i / 255.0) ** inv_gamma) * 255 for i in range(256)]).astype("uint8")
        image = cv2.LUT(image, table)

    # 4. Strict Safety Assertions
    assert image.shape == (128, 800), "Image shape altered by augmentation!"
    assert masks.shape == (4, 128, 800), "Mask shape altered by augmentation!"
    assert np.all(np.isin(masks, [0.0, 1.0])), "Mask values corrupted by interpolation!"

    return np.ascontiguousarray(image), np.ascontiguousarray(masks) 
 
 7. Common Mistakes and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Pitfall 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Practical Diagnostic 
 
 
 
 
 Independent Random Flips 
 Calling  RandomHorizontalFlip  on image and mask in separate calls. 
 Mask overlays appear on wrong side in 50% of augmented batches. 
 Plot augmented image with overlaid mask using matplotlib; verify visual alignment. 
 
 
 Mask Value Blurring 
 Using default bilinear interpolation in Albumentations or torchvision. 
 masks.max()  is 1.0, but  unique()  contains floats like  \(0.15, 0.43\) . 
 Assert  np.all(np.isin(masks, [0.0, 1.0])) . 
 
 
 Photometric Distortion of Masks 
 Passing masks into brightness or Gaussian noise functions. 
 Masks become noisy floating-point fields. 
 Verify that photometric transforms receive only  image=... . 
 
 
 Aspect Ratio Distortion 
 Using square resize (e.g.,  \(256 \times 256\)  or  \(512 \times 512\) ). 
 Longitudinal scratches widen unnaturally; spatial aliasing degrades thin defects. 
 Preserve native  \(128 \times 800\)  canvas throughout preprocessing. 
 
 
 
 
 8. Decisions You Must Make 
 
 Augmentation Probability Budget : Aggressive augmentations regularize models but can slow training convergence if applied excessively. 
 Start conservatively:  \(p_{\text{hflip}} = 0.5\) ,  \(p_{\text{vflip}} = 0.5\) . 
 Introduce subtle photometric adjustments (brightness  \(\pm 10\%\) , contrast  \(\pm 15\%\) ) only after your baseline achieves steady training convergence. 
 
 
 Validation Integrity :  Never apply augmentations to your validation partition . Validation must evaluate deterministic, uncorrupted ground truth images to provide reliable, reproducible benchmark scores across epochs. 
 
 
 9. Try It: Verify Dual Transform Consistency 
 Run this diagnostic snippet to verify that your augmentation helper maintains spatial alignment and preserves mask discreteness: 
 import numpy as np

# 1. Create a toy 128x800 strip with a defect at x in [100, 200]
toy_img = np.full((128, 800), 180, dtype=np.uint8)
toy_img[40:80, 100:200] = 50  # Dark defect

toy_masks = np.zeros((4, 128, 800), dtype=np.float32)
toy_masks[0, 40:80, 100:200] = 1.0  # Channel 0 defect_a

# 2. Apply horizontal reflection
flipped_img = np.fliplr(toy_img)
flipped_masks = np.flip(toy_masks, axis=2)

# 3. Check where the defect relocated
# Original: x in [100, 200) -> Width=800 -> Flipped: x in [800 - 200, 800 - 100) = [600, 700)
assert flipped_img[50, 650] == 50, "Image defect not at expected flipped location!"
assert flipped_masks[0, 50, 650] == 1.0, "Mask defect not aligned with flipped image!"
assert flipped_masks[0, 50, 150] == 0.0, "Old mask location should now be 0!"
assert np.all(np.isin(flipped_masks, [0.0, 1.0])), "Mask values corrupted!"

print("✓ Dual horizontal flip alignment and discreteness verified successfully!") 
 
 10. Authoritative Documentation & References 
 
 Albumentations Documentation :  Albumentations for Semantic Segmentation 
 PyTorch  torchvision.transforms.v2 :  Transforms v2 API (Image & Mask Alignment) 
 OpenCV Geometric Transformations & Interpolation :  OpenCV Geometric Transforms

title: Guide 04 · Validation Stratification
text:
Validation Strategy: Multi-Label Stratification for Rare Defect Detection 
 A reliable validation strategy is the compass of every machine learning project. If your validation score rises while your actual test performance falls, your compass is broken, and every subsequent engineering decision—from choosing architectures to tuning learning rates—will be guided by noise. 
 In industrial surface anomaly detection, establishing an honest validation split is especially challenging because  anomalies are rare events . Furthermore, our dataset is  multi-label : images can display zero, one, or multiple co-occurring defect classes. 
 In this guide, you will learn why naive random splitting causes extreme variance for rare defect categories, how  multi-label combination stratification  stabilizes validation metrics, and how to protect your pipeline against subtle data leakage. 
 
 1. Motivation: The "Split Lottery" of Rare Defects 
 Consider a dataset where one defect class—say,  defect_b —appears in only a small fraction of training images (for instance, around  \(2.7\%\)  prevalence). 
 Suppose you evaluate your model using a single  \(80/20\)  train/validation holdout (where  \(20\%\)  of images are held out for validation). If you partition images  purely at random , the number of positive  defect_b  images allocated to the validation set is a random variable drawn from a hypergeometric distribution. 
 The Variance of Random Sampling 
 Let  \(N\)  be the total number of images,  \(K\)  be the number of positive instances of a rare defect, and  \(n = 0.20 \times N\)  be the size of the validation partition. 
 The expected number of positive instances in validation is: 
 \[\mathbb{E}[X] = n \times \frac{K}{N} = 0.20 \times K\] 
 However, the standard deviation of this draw is: 
 \[\sigma = \sqrt{n \times \frac{K}{N} \times \left(1 - \frac{K}{N}\right) \times \frac{N - n}{N - 1}}\] 
 For a common class (where  \(K\)  is large),  \(\frac{\sigma}{\mathbb{E}[X]}\)  is small (perhaps  \(\pm 3\%\) ). But for an extremely rare class, the relative standard deviation  \(\frac{\sigma}{\mathbb{E}[X]}\)  can exceed  \(\pm 50\%\) ! 
 Random Holdout (The Split Lottery):
Draw A (Lucky Split):   Validation receives 1.6× the expected rare defects.
Draw B (Unlucky Split): Validation receives 0.4× the expected rare defects.
Draw C (Worst Case):    Validation receives ZERO rare defects! 
 If your validation partition receives zero or near-zero instances of a rare defect: 
 
 Per-class metrics (like Foreground Dice for  defect_b ) become undefined ( \(0/0\) ) or hyper-sensitive: a single misclassified pixel can collapse the score from  \(0.80\)  to  \(0.00\) . 
 Your validation score reflects  split luck , not model architecture or learning progress. 
 
 
 Figure 4.1: (A) Naive random holdout distribution across 1,000 simulations showing high variance and the risk of empty validation sets. (B) Multi-label combination stratification guaranteeing proportional representation across all defect combinations. 
 
 2. Multi-Label Combination Stratification 
 In standard single-label classification (e.g., ImageNet or MNIST),  StratifiedKFold  easily partitions classes by stratifying on the single target label. But in multi-label segmentation, each image possesses a vector of binary labels: 
 \[\mathbf{y}_i = [y_{\text{defect\_a}}, y_{\text{defect\_b}}, y_{\text{defect\_c}}, y_{\text{defect\_d}}] \in \{0, 1\}^4\] 
 With 4 binary classes, there are  \(2^4 = 16\)  possible combinations: 
 Possible Defect Combination Signatures:
• "clean"                 (no defect present)
• "defect_a"              (isolated defect a)
• "defect_b"              (isolated defect b)
• "defect_c"              (isolated defect c)
• "defect_d"              (isolated defect d)
• "defect_a+defect_c"     (co-occurring a and c)
• "defect_b+defect_c"     (co-occurring b and c)
... up to all 4 co-occurring 
 The Combination Stratification Algorithm 
 To guarantee balanced representation without distorting co-occurrence patterns: 
 
 Group by Image ID : Condense the 4 rows of  train.csv  per image into a single record. 
 Compute the Combination Signature : For each image, create an alphabetical string indicating all active defect categories (or  "clean"  if no defect is present). 
 Partition Stratified by Signature : Allocate the holdout within each combination stratum so that the validation set receives the exact same proportion of clean images, single defects, and rare multi-defect pairs as the full dataset. 
 
 # Constructing the Combination Signature
def get_combination_signatures(df):
    # Filter to active defect annotations
    active = df[df["mask_rle"].str.strip() != ""]
    # Group by image and join sorted defect names
    signatures = active.groupby("image_id")["defect_type"].apply(lambda s: "+".join(sorted(s)))
    # Map back to all image IDs (unannotated images become 'clean')
    all_signatures = pd.Series(index=df["image_id"].unique(), data="clean", dtype=object)
    all_signatures.update(signatures)
    return all_signatures 
 
 3. The Edge Case: Singleton Combinations 
 When you inspect the combination distribution in real-world industrial data, you will discover that some multi-defect combinations are  extremely rare —appearing in only 1, 2, or 3 images across the entire dataset! 
 \[\text{What do you do if combination } \text{"defect_a+defect_b+defect_d"} \text{ has exactly } 1 \text{ sample?}\] 
 Mathematically, you cannot split a single sample into an  \(80\%\)  train and  \(20\%\)  validation slice. You must establish a deterministic rule: 
 
 Rule Option A (Train Priority) : Allocate singletons ( \(N=1\) ) to the  training partition . Rationale: The neural network cannot learn a complex multi-defect interaction if it never sees it during training. 
 Rule Option B (Iterative Stratification) : Use an algorithm like Sechidis et al.'s  Iterative Multi-label Stratification , which greedily optimizes marginal label distributions rather than exact combination strings. 
 
 Whichever rule you adopt, document it explicitly and fix your random seed ( seed=42 ) so that your split is  \(100\%\)  reproducible across runs. 
 
 4. Preventing Data Leakage: The Verification Checklist 
 Data leakage occurs when information from outside the training dataset is used to create or tune the model. In segmentation pipelines, leakage takes several subtle forms: 
 1. Image-Level Isolation Check 
 Never allow an image ID to appear in both training and validation sets: 
 \[\text{Train}_{\text{IDs}} \cap \text{Val}_{\text{IDs}} = \emptyset\] 
 2. Preprocessing & Normalization Leakage 
 If you normalize images using dataset mean  \(\mu\)  and standard deviation  \(\sigma\) : 
 
 WRONG : Computing  \(\mu\)  and  \(\sigma\)  across all 11,393 images in  data/public/train/ . (The validation set leaks into your training statistics!) 
 CORRECT : Computing  \(\mu\)  and  \(\sigma\)  strictly on your  \(80\%\)  training partition, then applying those exact frozen parameters to normalize the  \(20\%\)  validation partition. 
 
 3. Holdout Overfitting (Validation Degradation) 
 If you train 50 different model variations and repeatedly tune decision thresholds or minimum-area filters to maximize the score on your single  \(20\%\)  validation holdout, you will  overfit the validation set . 
 
 The validation score will steadily climb from  \(0.62\)  to  \(0.71\) , but your performance on the hidden Kaggle test leaderboard will fail to improve. 
 Defense : Reserve threshold searches for candidate models only, or adopt  \(5\) -fold cross-validation when conducting extensive hyperparameter sweeps. 
 
 
 5. Single Holdout vs. 5-Fold Cross-Validation 
 
 
 
 Property 
 Single  \(80/20\)  Holdout 
 5-Fold Cross-Validation 
 
 
 
 
 Training Budget 
 \(1\times\)  training time (Fast iteration) 
 \(5\times\)  training time (Substantial compute) 
 
 
 Validation Size 
 \(20\%\)  of training data 
 \(100\%\)  of data evaluated out-of-fold (OOF) 
 
 
 Variance on Rare Classes 
 Low (if combination-stratified), but fixed 
 Averaged across all 5 folds; highly robust 
 
 
 Ensembling 
 Single model inference 
 Natural 5-model ensemble for test predictions 
 
 
 Recommended Stage 
 Milestone 2 Baseline Pipeline 
 Milestone 3 Advanced Modeling 
 
 
 
 For Milestone 2, a single combination-stratified  \(80/20\)  holdout provides the optimal balance of speed, stability, and fast debugging. 
 
 6. Common Mistakes and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Pitfall 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Practical Diagnostic 
 
 
 
 
 Duplicate Image IDs 
 Failing to deduplicate image IDs when creating splits. 
 Same image ID appears in both partitions. 
 Assert  len(set(train_ids) & set(val_ids)) == 0 . 
 
 
 Unstratified Split 
 Calling standard  KFold  or random sampling. 
 Validation set receives 0 positive samples for rare defect. 
 Check  val_df[val_df['defect_type'] == 'defect_b']['mask_rle'].count() > 0 . 
 
 
 Leaked Normalization 
 Calculating Z-score mean/std on all images combined. 
 Small optimistic score bias; poor test generalizability. 
 Save normalization parameters from  train_df  only. 
 
 
 Unfixed Random Seed 
 Not setting  random_state=42  in split generator. 
 Training and validation partitions shift on every script execution! 
 Verify that  hash(tuple(sorted(val_ids)))  is identical across runs. 
 
 
 
 
 7. Decisions You Must Make 
 
 Holdout Ratio : Standard ratios are  \(80/20\)  (9,114 train / 2,279 val) or  \(85/15\) . Choose a ratio that leaves at least 50+ positive samples of your rarest defect in validation. 
 Stratification Granularity : Will you stratify on exact combination strings (e.g.,  "defect_a+defect_c" ), or will you use an iterative multi-label stratification library? 
 Artifact Persistence : Save your split assignments to a CSV file (e.g.,  reports/folds.csv  or  splits/holdout.csv  containing  image_id,split ) so that every subsequent experiment loads the  exact same partition . 
 
 
 8. Try It: Build a Combination Stratified Split on Toy Data 
 Run this self-contained script to observe how combination stratification balances rare classes across a toy dataset of 10 fictional images: 
 import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedShuffleSplit

# 1. Create toy dataset of 10 images with combination labels
# Image 0..4: clean; Image 5..7: common defect c; Image 8..9: rare defect b
toy_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "image_id": [f"STRIP_{i:04d}" for i in range(10)],
    "combo": ["clean"] * 5 + ["defect_c"] * 3 + ["defect_b"] * 2
})

print("Full Toy Distribution:")
print(toy_data["combo"].value_counts())

# 2. Stratified 80/20 split (8 train, 2 val)
splitter = StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
train_idx, val_idx = next(splitter.split(toy_data, toy_data["combo"]))

train_set = toy_data.iloc[train_idx]
val_set = toy_data.iloc[val_idx]

print("\nTrain Partition (8 images):")
print(train_set["combo"].value_counts())

print("\nValidation Partition (2 images):")
print(val_set["combo"].value_counts())

# Assertions
assert len(val_set) == 2
assert "defect_b" in val_set["combo"].values, "Rare defect missing from validation!"
assert len(set(train_set["image_id"]) & set(val_set["image_id"])) == 0, "Leakage detected!"
print("\n✓ Stratified split verified: rare class represented, zero leakage!") 
 
 9. Authoritative Documentation & References 
 
 Sechidis et al. (2011) :  On the Stratification of Multi-Label Data 
 Scikit-Learn  StratifiedShuffleSplit :  Scikit-Learn Splitter Documentation 
 Iterative Stratification Library :  Iterative-Stratification on GitHub

title: Guide 05 · W&B Experiment Tracking
text:
Experiment Tracking with Weights & Biases 
 In machine learning research and Kaggle competitions, raw intuition is not enough. You will iterate across multiple model architectures (U-Net, FPN, DeepLabV3+), test diverse loss functions (BCE, Dice, Focal), evaluate different learning rate schedules, and sweep decision thresholds. 
 If you track these experiments using terminal printouts, text files, or manual spreadsheets, critical details will inevitably slip through the cracks:  Which learning rate produced that 0.65 Dice score? Did that checkpoint use horizontal flips? What did the predicted masks look like when recall collapsed on defect_b? 
 Weights & Biases (W&B)  provides an experiment tracking platform that automatically records configurations, synchronizes training and validation metrics, archives model checkpoints as versioned artifacts, and renders interactive qualitative segmentation overlays. 
 This guide teaches the complete lifecycle of a W&B tracking workflow, emphasizes  step alignment and fair comparisons , and details  safe credential handling . 
 
 1. Motivation: The Experiment Tracking Lifecycle 
 A deep learning experiment is more than just final validation numbers. It is a reproducible record consisting of: 
 
 Inputs : Code version (git commit), dataset partition hash, hyperparameters, random seeds. 
 Process : Training dynamics, loss curves, gradient norms, learning rate decay. 
 Outputs : Quantitative validation metrics (per-class Dice, IoU, empty-image accuracy), qualitative mask overlays, and saved model weights. 
 
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                             The W&B Run Cycle                               │
├─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┤
│    1. Initialize    │       2. Log Epoch        │        3. Finalize        │
│  wandb.init(...)    │   wandb.log({metrics})    │      wandb.finish()       │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
│ • Model config      │ • Train loss (BCE, Dice)  │ • Log best model artifact │
│ • Hyperparameters   │ • Val Dice & IoU per-class│ • Record run summary      │
│ • Split seed & fold │ • Qualitative mask images │ • Flush telemetry buffer  │
└─────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘ 
 
 Figure 5.1: Weights & Biases run lifecycle: configuration logging, synchronized metric tracking, qualitative mask overlay inspection, and versioned model artifact storage. 
 
 2. Safe Credential Handling: Never Hardcode API Keys 
 When setting up W&B, students frequently make a critical security mistake: pasting their raw W&B API key directly into Python scripts or Jupyter notebooks: 
 # CRITICAL SECURITY VULNERABILITY - NEVER DO THIS!
wandb.login(key="d83f98234a...")  # If committed to git or shared, your account is exposed! 
 The Three Safe Credential Protocols: 
 Protocol 1: Environment Variables (Recommended for Local Machines) 
 Set your API key in your terminal shell environment before executing Python:
 export WANDB_API_KEY="your_private_api_key_here"
uv run python src/train.py 
Inside Python,  wandb.init()  will automatically detect the environment variable without any key appearing in your code. 
 Protocol 2: Kaggle Secrets (Recommended for Cloud Notebooks) 
 In Kaggle Notebooks: 
 
 Navigate to  Add-ons   \(\to\)   Secrets . 
 Add a new secret with Label  WANDB_API_KEY  and your key as the Value. 
 In your notebook initialization cell:
    from kaggle_secrets import UserSecretsClient
import wandb
user_secrets = UserSecretsClient()
wandb_api_key = user_secrets.get_secret("WANDB_API_KEY")
wandb.login(key=wandb_api_key) 
 
 Protocol 3: Offline Mode (Recommended for Air-Gapped or Quick Smoke Tests) 
 If you are developing offline or running quick 1-epoch sanity checks, disable network communication entirely:
 export WANDB_MODE="offline"
# Or inside Python:
os.environ["WANDB_MODE"] = "offline" 
W&B will record all metrics, charts, and artifacts locally to a  wandb/  folder on disk without attempting to contact external servers. You can later sync offline runs using  wandb sync wandb/offline-run-... . 
 
 3. Configuration & Metadata Logging 
 Before training begins, log every hyperparameter and environment variable required to reproduce the run. 
 import wandb

config = {
    # Architecture
    "architecture": "unet",
    "encoder_backbone": "resnet34",
    "encoder_weights": "imagenet",
    "in_channels": 1,
    "num_classes": 4,
    "head_type": "sigmoid",  # or "softmax"

    # Optimization
    "epochs": 15,
    "batch_size": 8,
    "learning_rate": 1e-3,
    "weight_decay": 1e-4,
    "lr_scheduler": "cosine",
    "loss_function": "bce_dice_combo",

    # Dataset & Partition
    "image_shape": [128, 800],
    "train_split_ratio": 0.8,
    "split_seed": 42,
    "data_version": "v1.0_clean",
}

run = wandb.init(
    project="industrial-surface-anomaly-segmentation",
    name="unet-resnet34-baseline-fold0",
    config=config,
    notes="Initial baseline training with BCE+Dice loss on combination-stratified holdout.",
    tags=["baseline", "unet", "fold0"],
) 
 
 4. Metric Synchronization: The Step Axis Trap 
 A frequent source of broken, unreadable W&B dashboards is  mismatched step axes . 
 By default, every call to  wandb.log(...)  increments an internal integer counter called  _step . If you log batch-level training losses inside your inner loop and epoch-level validation metrics in your outer loop: 
 
 Batch training losses are logged at steps  \(1, 2, 3, \dots, 500\) . 
 Validation metrics are logged at step  \(501\)  (labeled epoch 1). 
 Subsequent batch losses resume at steps  \(502, \dots, 1000\) . 
 
 The resulting W&B charts become jagged, discontinuous, or out-of-sync. 
 The Correct Pattern: Explicit Step Synchronization 
 Define an explicit step axis—typically  epoch —or log a consolidated metric dictionary at the end of each epoch: 
 for epoch in range(1, num_epochs + 1):
    train_loss, train_bce, train_dice = train_one_epoch(model, train_loader, optimizer, criterion)
    val_loss, val_dice_mean, val_dice_per_class = validate_one_epoch(model, val_loader, criterion)

    # Log everything together with an explicit step parameter
    wandb.log({
        "epoch": epoch,
        "train/loss_total": train_loss,
        "train/loss_bce": train_bce,
        "train/loss_dice": train_dice,
        "val/loss_total": val_loss,
        "val/dice_mean": val_dice_mean,
        "val/dice_defect_a": val_dice_per_class[0],
        "val/dice_defect_b": val_dice_per_class[1],
        "val/dice_defect_c": val_dice_per_class[2],
        "val/dice_defect_d": val_dice_per_class[3],
        "learning_rate": optimizer.param_groups[0]["lr"],
    }, step=epoch) 
 Using namespaced prefixes (like  train/  and  val/ ) groups related curves into clean panels in the W&B web interface. 
 
 5. Visualizing Predictions: Segmentation Mask Overlays 
 Numbers and loss curves only tell part of the story. A model might achieve a high mean Dice score solely by predicting empty masks on clean images, while failing to detect subtle defects. 
 W&B natively supports  interactive segmentation overlays  using  wandb.Image : 
 def log_validation_mask_predictions(model, val_loader, epoch, device, max_samples=4):
    model.eval()
    images_to_log = []

    class_labels = {
        0: "background",
        1: "defect_a",
        2: "defect_b",
        3: "defect_c",
        4: "defect_d"
    }

    with torch.no_grad():
        for batch in val_loader:
            imgs = batch["image"].to(device)
            masks = batch["mask"].cpu().numpy()  # Ground truth [B, 4, 128, 800]
            logits = model(imgs)
            probs = torch.sigmoid(logits).cpu().numpy()  # Predicted [B, 4, 128, 800]

            for i in range(min(len(imgs), max_samples)):
                # Convert normalized grayscale tensor back to [0, 255] uint8 for display
                raw_img = (imgs[i, 0].cpu().numpy() * 0.25 + 0.5) * 255.0
                raw_img = np.clip(raw_img, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

                # Create discrete 2D map for GT and Prediction (channel index 1..4)
                gt_2d = np.zeros((128, 800), dtype=np.uint8)
                for c in range(4):
                    gt_2d[masks[i, c] > 0.5] = c + 1

                pred_2d = np.zeros((128, 800), dtype=np.uint8)
                for c in range(4):
                    pred_2d[probs[i, c] >= 0.5] = c + 1

                # Assemble W&B Image with mask overlay
                wb_img = wandb.Image(
                    raw_img,
                    masks={
                        "ground_truth": {"mask_data": gt_2d, "class_labels": class_labels},
                        "prediction":   {"mask_data": pred_2d, "class_labels": class_labels},
                    },
                    caption=f"Sample {batch['image_id'][i]} (Epoch {epoch})"
                )
                images_to_log.append(wb_img)
            break  # Only log first batch

    wandb.log({"val/qualitative_masks": images_to_log}, step=epoch) 
 In the W&B UI, this allows you to toggle ground truth vs. predicted masks, adjust transparency, and inspect exactly how predictions evolve from epoch 1 to epoch 15. 
 
 6. Model Artifacts: Saving Checkpoints with Lineage 
 Rather than saving untracked  .pt  files to arbitrary local directories, log your best checkpoints as  W&B Artifacts : 
 def save_model_artifact(checkpoint_path: str, model_name: str, val_score: float, epoch: int):
    artifact = wandb.Artifact(
        name=f"{model_name}-best",
        type="model",
        description=f"Best model checkpoint at epoch {epoch} with Val Dice {val_score:.4f}",
        metadata={"val_dice": val_score, "epoch": epoch}
    )
    # Add checkpoint file
    artifact.add_file(checkpoint_path)
    # Log and track version in W&B
    wandb.log_artifact(artifact) 
 Advantages: 
 
 Checkpoints are cryptographically hashed (SHA256) and versioned ( v0 ,  v1 ,  v2 ,  latest ). 
 Every model checkpoint is linked directly to the training run, git commit, and hyperparameters that produced it. 
 Downstream inference scripts can download the exact winning checkpoint directly using  run.use_artifact(...) . 
 
 
 7. The Fair Comparison Protocol 
 When comparing two runs in W&B (e.g., Run A:  U-Net ResNet34  vs. Run B:  U-Net EfficientNet-B0 ): 
                                 FAIR COMPARISON PROTOCOL
┌───────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┐
│              PERMITTED                │              FORBIDDEN                │
├───────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┤
│ • Different model architecture        │ • Different validation split IDs      │
│ • Different learning rate / optimizer │ • Different metric formulas           │
│ • Different loss weightings           │ • Different image normalization       │
│ • Different augmentation strengths    │ • Comparing local smoke to full fold  │
└───────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────┘ 
 If Run A evaluated on a random split with 15 instances of  defect_b , while Run B evaluated on a split with 40 instances of  defect_b ,  their validation scores cannot be compared . Only runs evaluated on the exact same combination-stratified partition provide an honest scientific comparison. 
 
 8. Common Mistakes and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Failure Mode 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Practical Diagnostic 
 
 
 
 
 Leaked Credentials 
 Hardcoding  wandb.login(key="...")  in scripts. 
 Security alert or compromised account. 
 Check code for raw strings; use  os.environ["WANDB_API_KEY"] . 
 
 
 Sawtooth Metric Charts 
 Logging train metrics and val metrics on unsynchronized steps. 
 Charts jump back and forth along the x-axis. 
 Pass explicit  step=epoch  to every  wandb.log(...)  call. 
 
 
 Zombie / Hanging Runs 
 Forgetting to call  wandb.finish()  before script exits. 
 Run appears active indefinitely on dashboard. 
 Place  wandb.finish()  in a  try...finally  block. 
 
 
 Network Timeout on Save 
 Uploading 500 MB model artifacts over slow internet. 
 Script freezes at end of training. 
 Save checkpoint locally first; upload asynchronously or save only  best.pt . 
 
 
 Excessive Media Logging 
 Logging 100+ images on every batch. 
 Disk fills up; dashboard slows to a crawl. 
 Restrict qualitative image logging to 4–8 fixed canaries per epoch. 
 
 
 
 
 9. Try It: Simulate an Offline W&B Tracking Loop 
 Run this self-contained script to verify that W&B logs configuration, metrics, and summaries in offline mode without requiring internet access or credentials: 
 import os
import wandb

# 1. Force offline mode
os.environ["WANDB_MODE"] = "offline"

# 2. Initialize tracking run
run = wandb.init(
    project="milestone2-diagnostic",
    name="synthetic-offline-test",
    config={"lr": 1e-3, "batch_size": 8, "architecture": "toy-unet"}
)

# 3. Simulate 3 training epochs
for ep in range(1, 4):
    simulated_train_loss = 0.8 / ep
    simulated_val_dice = 0.5 + 0.1 * ep

    wandb.log({
        "epoch": ep,
        "train/loss": simulated_train_loss,
        "val/dice_mean": simulated_val_dice,
    }, step=ep)

# 4. Finalize run
wandb.finish()

print("✓ Offline W&B tracking loop executed and finalized successfully!")
